contributions.statement: When an LLM judge scores agent runs, generate a rubric per task (hidden from the agent) and average at least three judge samples. Do not treat the judge as a human proxy: rubric-judge agreement with experts was τ≈0.19, below expert-expert agreement of 0.30.
contributions.evidence: Figure 3: three rubric-judge samples reach the noise share of eight baseline-judge samples (16 GRPO groups); disputed-pair test p=0.109.

contributions.statement: A director model can drive an unmodified coding CLI through a non-interactive wrapper with per-call deadlines, partial transcripts on timeout, and resumable sessions. A director trained against a cheap coding model benefited when a stronger one was swapped in.
contributions.evidence: §3.4 CAT wrapper; Appendix A.2 tool swap (four rollouts per task); Appendix B.2 no-tool ablation collapsed (single run).

contributions.statement: Automated prompt optimisation of a frontier coding agent did not reach the gain from post-training the director.
contributions.evidence: Figure 5 left: 24 generations of Claude-driven prompt rewriting on Codex.

reason: Only the judge-noise practice transfers: averaging several samples of a per-task rubric judge cuts noise, and its weak human agreement is quantified. That helps any team scoring agent runs with an LLM. The CAT pattern and the prompt-vs-training result require RL post-training, which this team will not do.
